entries.title: reach what the AES kernels leave in vector registers (AEAD-4), and settle --cpu for the kernel path
entries.body: Each AES kernel in runtime/runtime-aes.c (the key schedule, CTR, GHASH and the single block) now ends in nish_aes_clear, a noinline asm routine that zeroes every caller-saved vector register and the general registers the kernels use, so round keys, H's powers, counter and keystream blocks no longer stay in registers after a seal or open. A new check reads each kernel's -O2 disassembly on x86-64, aarch64 and x86-64-v3, requires every register a kernel touched to be cleared before each ret and every vector spill to be wiped, and refuses a twin without the clear and a twin whose clear skips one register. AEAD-4 is narrowed to what is still out of reach (the -O0 debug profile, and the bitsliced path's stack) and records why --cpu does not pick the kernel path at build time: no x86-64 psABI level guarantees AES-NI or PCLMULQDQ, so the runtime check stays. The runtime-aes.c text budget moves from 2,560 to 2,816 bytes for the clear.

entries.title: add nish/page/frame, a framebuffer presenter and fixed-step loop
entries.body:
A page can now put a wasm module's 0xRRGGBB framebuffer on a canvas through WebGPU, WebGL 2 or Canvas 2D. It uses whichever tier answers first, records why each refused, and moves down a tier when a device or context is lost at runtime. A refused tier releases what it held, and a tier that needs a fresh canvas swaps it in place and hands it to onFallback, so a page can re-attach its listeners.

runFixedStep steps a simulation at a fixed rate and renders on every animation frame with an interpolation alpha, so a 240 Hz display gets 240 distinct frames. A long frame counts as at most a quarter second, and at most 8 steps run per frame.

It is the page half of the standard library, shipped as plain ESM with no imports as nish/page/frame, and documented under "In a browser" in the interop guide.

entries.title: a QUIC transfer survives a NAT rebind while one hole fills the stream buffer
entries.body:
A stream's send buffer is maxStreamData bytes. Once one packet of it was lost, the server could send nothing new until the resend was acknowledged, so between the client's ACK of that resend and the burst it freed, nothing was on its way to the client. A NAT rebinding in that gap was never seen: the client had nothing to answer, every later packet (the PTO probe included) went to the old binding, and the transfer stalled until the idle timeout. The fix is an earlier ACK-eliciting probe, sent max(sRTT/2, 1 ms) after the last ACK-eliciting packet while a stream's buffer is full behind bytes in flight and nothing of it is left to send, at most once per acknowledgement that advances the Application Data space and never while the sent ring is full. The client's ACK of it comes from its new port and the connection follows. The send buffer stays tied to maxStreamData, now documented as the memory bound of a stream's send side on room(), QuicServerConfig.maxStreamData and in docs/security/quic.md (QUIC-12, with what remains: a half round trip with the NAT beside the client, up to two full datagrams a round trip outside the window, and a ~166 ms probe delay after a validated migration until the new path's first RTT sample).

Fixes #1485
tests: tests/link/net_interop_server/rebind.ts (a timed 256 KiB transfer at maxStreamData 64 KiB through a NAT rebinding in the gap: the server follows at 90 ms and the transfer finishes by 405 ms; without the probe the server never follows and the client gives up)

entries.title: a process.spawn grant that lets a program start helpers
entries.body:
Under --sandbox, every program a dependency's process.spawn=<program> grant starts gets exactly one exec (#1486), so a granted program cannot start helpers. A grant can now opt a program out: "process.spawn=exec:<program>" grants the program as process.spawn=<program> does and lets it and its descendants execute anything the exec allowlist reaches, which includes every granted program's loader, so such a program can run anything. Grant it only to a dependency that may run anything; a plainly granted program beside it is still held to its one exec.

The rule is by file identity: the compiler writes an exec: entry as ///<path> in the allowlist, the runtime records that file's identity before confinement, and a spawn whose opened target is that file (any name for it, a hard link included) starts without the one-exec filter, still through the identity-checked, private-descriptor path. A program granted both ways is exec:. "process.spawn=exec:" with no program is refused (NL3046), a literal an exec: grant does not cover is refused like any narrow grant (NL2594), and a capabilities lock file that recorded the plain grant refuses an added exec: prefix (NL2593). A build without exec: grants is unchanged.

entries.title: an HTTP/3 server clock (H3-5) and WebTransport's rate-cap decision
entries.body:
An HTTP/3 server now closes a slot whose client holds it without progress, with no code in the program. Two new Http3Config fields, headTimeout (30 s by default) and idleTimeout (60 s), are checked at start-up. A connection with no request open past idleTimeout closes with H3_NO_ERROR, and one whose client trickles a request's head past headTimeout closes with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD. The clock starts on the first next() that finds the handshake chose h3, so neither a peer's transport parameters (a client that allows fewer than three unidirectional streams) nor a slot the program runs another protocol on (the interop server's hq-interop) changes when it runs; a slot the program never calls next() on is left to QUIC's idle timeout. A request whose head has arrived is the program's to time. The head clock runs from when the connection last completed a head, so a client completing heads faster than headTimeout can hold another stream's HEADERS open, bounded by maxStreamsBidi; H3-5's record says so. HTTP3_SERVER_SLOT_BYTES grows for the clock's fields.

WebTransport's maxDatagramsPerSecond keeps dropping and counting what passes the cap and never closes the session: datagrams are unreliable by contract (RFC 9297), a drop costs O(1), and a close would punish a bursty browser. WT-2 records that as the defence.

entries.title: P-256's cached table for G and a safegcd scalar inverse for verify (K5)
entries.body:
P-256 sign and key generation now compute k·G from a fixed-base table generated once by scripts/gen-p256-table.mjs (the work of #1487, which this supersedes), and verify takes its public s^-1 through the constant-time safegcd scalar inverse instead of a Fermat ladder. The scratch the comb uses widens, which moves the IR of the TLS, HTTP and QUIC programs; nish-cmp declares those moves.

Supersedes #1487.

* ci: reuse the compiler under test when nothing it is linked from changed

Every `node tests/run.js` linked src/compile.ts with the seed before its first
check: two seconds of front end and about 69 of the speed profile's full LTO on
one core, since a target with landing pads links in one partition. Each of the
eight `test` shards paid it, the NEON job paid it seven times (once per
`node tests/run.js` step), and so did every filtered run at a workstation.

tests/self/compiler-cache.js now keeps the binary in
build/cache/compiler-under-test/ under a hash of everything the link reads: the
seed and its package (libexec/, runtime/, std/, scripts/build.sh, from the root
the compiler's own package search settles on), this checkout's src/, std/ and
package.json, the C compiler and linker versions, CC, NISH_SQLITE_CFLAGS, the
platform, architecture and core count. A run with the same inputs copies the
binary instead of linking it; the first check says which it did. The key is
coarser than the link, so it can miss when nothing relevant changed, but it
never reuses a binary built from different inputs. A seed run under Node is
never kept, and scripts/bootstrap.sh and the fixed point never read the cache.

In CI, .github/actions/compiler-cache computes the key, restores that entry
through the Actions cache, links or copies the compiler, and saves a miss (one
matrix row saves). The `test`, `runner`, NEON, `runtime-net` and Apple-silicon
SHA-256 jobs use it.

entries.title: answer static routes from an exact-path table ahead of the trie walk (WP49 stage 6)
entries.body:
A route with no parameter and no `*` is now also filed under a hash of
its method and path, and `Router.match` looks there before it walks the
tree: one pass over the path, at most eight slots, and a byte comparison
for a slot whose method and length agree. The tree stays the definition.

tree's, and anything the table does not hold falls through unchanged.
`matchTree` is the tree alone, and the tests hold `match` to it on every
route, near miss, query and table growth.

A client adds nothing to the table and a lookup's cost is bounded by the
longest static route, whatever the target (docs/security/router.md,
ROUTE-10 to ROUTE-12). The one unchecked read is the static path compare
over the private table; the method compare stays checked, since the
method arrays are public.

The standard library gains the Nish half of a small browser-game kit.

entries.title: enum narrowing builds an enum's members once
entries.body:
Narrowing an enum variable on `x.kind === K.A`, `!==` and at `||`/`&&` joins
re-interned every member of the enum on each test, through a string-keyed
table, and compared member lists pairwise. With a 79-member enum that made
checking enum-heavy code 26% more expensive than the same code on i32
constants.

The checker now builds each enum's member list once, looks member ids up by
(enum, value) without a string key, holds a narrowed set compactly as
"exactly these members" or "all members except these", and only materialises
a full ordered list where something enumerates or prints it. Member types are
still created where they were before, so an enum with two members of one
value is named in diagnostics exactly as it was. Diagnostics, narrowed types
and emitted IR are unchanged.
metrics: callgrind instructions checking src/ (compile.ts -o dir/); main's compiler: i32 node kinds 4,832,180,422, enum node kinds 6,111,521,373 (+26.5%); this compiler: i32 4,830,970,824, enum 4,858,669,843 (+0.57%); deterministic counts, IR byte-identical across compilers on both trees

entries.title: close the HTTP, WebSocket, YAML and PKI attack paths and pin CI to Node 26 LTS
entries.body:
Fixes the vulnerability classes from this year's advisories that reached Nish's own implementations: HTTP/1 chunk-extension smuggling and malformed Host, HTTP/2 SETTINGS-flood CPU amplification, HTTP/3 rapid reset, cross-site WebSocket hijacking (a new origin check), YAML merge-key alias blow-up, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 name-constraint bypass. A caller can now pass distrusted keys to the PKI chain builder. Each fix lands with a before/after test and its docs/security/ record.

CI and release move to Node 26.13.1 LTS (the diverse double-compiling chain stays on 22.23.4, because npm 11 refuses old lockfiles). Every npm ci runs with --ignore-scripts, guarded by a lint check that fails when a locked package gains an install script. The seed fetch fails when it cannot verify the build attestation. The release job installs nothing and restores no shared cache, and CODEOWNERS covers the workflows.

entries.title: an update notice and `nish upgrade`
entries.body:
A compile, `nish --version` or `nish --help` on a terminal now ends with one
line on stderr when a newer release is out: `nish X is available (you have Y);
run `nish upgrade``. The line is read from a cache under
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/nish/release` (else `~/.cache/nish/release`), which is
believed only when it is a private file this user owns in a private
directory this user owns. A check detached in the background refreshes it at
most once a day, with a 2 s limit, and a failure is silent. The notice is
never shown when stderr is not a terminal, with `--json`, with `CI` or
`NISH_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` set, in `nish run`, or after a usage error. Stdout and
the exit status never change.

`nish upgrade` installs the latest release, or a named one, through that
tag's own `install.sh`, so its checksum and attestation checks apply. With no
version it never moves to an older or equal release. `nish upgrade --check`
prints the current and latest versions (exit 3 when the latest cannot be
found). An npm install is pointed at `npm install -g nish@<version>` and a
build from a checkout is refused, both with exit 2. A version that is not a
plain release version is refused before any network access.

Programs can ask the same questions through the new `nish/release` module:
the latest release from GitHub's `/releases/latest` redirect (only a redirect
to that repository's release tag is accepted), semver comparison, and a
trusted once-a-day cache.
metrics: no added time with stderr not a terminal (1.5-1.7 ms per `nish --version` either way, within noise); ~3.3 ms on a terminal (the trust probe), +-0.3 ms over 200 runs; none with NISH_NO_UPDATE_CHECK or CI

entries.title: the AST node kinds become a NodeKind enum
entries.body:

node-kind signature are typed `NodeKind`. Nish-0, the subset src/ is written

language's own rule. N_COUNT, which nothing read, is gone.

Members are PascalCase, the old name without `N_` (`NodeKind.TypeRef`), so a

nodeName's strings, and so --emit-ast, are unchanged.

The enum's narrowing proved one check could never be false
(`initializer.kind !== N_EMPTY` in checkVariableList), and it is dropped. The
compiler's own IR is otherwise byte-identical: built by the seed, every module
but statements.ll matches main, and statements.ll loses only that check.

entries.title: raise the soft descriptor limit to the hard limit in nish:net
entries.body:
A native server was held to the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE it inherited, often 1024
(256 on macOS), though the hard limit is usually far higher, so it refused
connections with -24 long before the operator's limit. The first nish:net call
that creates a descriptor (a socket, a socket pair or a poller) now raises the
soft limit to the hard one, once per process, as Node and Go do at start-up.
On macOS it stops at OPEN_MAX, or below that where kern.maxfilesperproc is
lower. A failed raise is ignored and the program keeps the limit it had.
Children started by spawn inherit the raised limit. Going past the hard limit
stays the operator's call (ulimit -Hn, LimitNOFILE=, the container's nofile).

Recorded as RT-54 in docs/security/runtime.md; getrlimit and setrlimit are
reserved in src/c-symbols.ts. runtime-net.c's .text is 4977 of its 5120 byte
budget.

Tests: tests/link/net_fd_limit (under ulimit -S -n 64 a program that has
called tcpListen holds 200 more descriptors; before the fix pollCreate
answered -24 after 60), tests/link/net_handler_descriptors (now run under
ulimit -n 1024, so it still meets the limit fast)
Fixes #1543

entries.title: print async_cancel's lines in an order no clock decides
entries.body:

entries.title: pin SQLite's sub-second lock-wait backoff in the default build
entries.body: The vendored SQLite 3.54.1 already waits on a busy lock in 1 to 100 ms steps in the default build. Its busy handler keys on HAVE_NANOSLEEP, which is on unless defined to 0, not on HAVE_USLEEP as older SQLite did, so adding -DHAVE_USLEEP to the defaults would change no object. A new link program, tests/link/sqlite_busy_backoff, holds a write lock on one connection and sets busy_timeout = 300 on a second. It checks that the blocked write returns SQLITE_BUSY after at least 250 ms and under 900 ms. The whole-second handler returns at once for any timeout under a second, so a SQLite update that brings it back fails the test. docs/security/sqlite.md records why HAVE_USLEEP is absent and names the test.

entries.title: finish a Content-Length response once its whole body is sent
entries.body:
An Http1Connection response stayed owed until the program called end(), even after write or sendBody had sent every byte its Content-Length declared. A program that skipped end() left a keep-alive connection waiting forever: the client read a complete response, and its next request on the connection was never answered, with no error anywhere.

The connection now treats a response as finished when it looks for the next request, if that response has sent its whole declared length or carries no body at all (Content-Length 0, HEAD, 204, 304). end() is optional for those. A chunked body, and an unframed one to an HTTP/1.0 client, has no length the connection can count, so it still ends only at end(), and the docs say so. A program that calls end() before the next request starts gets the same answers and the same bytes on the wire as before; one that calls it after the connection has moved on gets H1_CLOSED, as a second end() always did.

entries.title: shrink what an idle Http1Server connection holds
entries.body:
An idle keep-alive Http1Server connection now holds 904 bytes of arena on the default config, against 3,384 on the base for a slot that has served four requests and parked.

- Http1Config.idleInput is now on by default. A parked slot lends its parser input and head buffers back to the server's pools between requests. Those views stay valid only until the next `next()`, as the module already documents.
- Http1Connection and Http1Parser start with shared empty arrays where no write site can push to them.
- The constructor no longer builds a throwaway HttpDate; build() passes the shared one in.
- The 64-entry spans array is made on the first field line.
- The kept response head is sized to what it holds, not a fixed 1 KiB.
- Http1OutputPool.take reserves room in its free list when it makes a buffer, so give never allocates after warm-up and a serve loop's arena stays flat.

tests/runtime-budgets.js pins the idle figure with HTTP1_SERVER_IDLE_BYTES = 1024, checked by the net_http1_server startup program. The bench README and docs/security/http1-codec.md record the measurements, the new default and why the lent buffers' lifetime keeps it safe.
metrics: 904 B per idle connection (arena, default config, four GETs then parked), against 3,384 B on the base; keep-alive plaintext, json and post-json throughput with idleInput on stay inside the 12–17% copy-to-copy noise band of bench/http1-conn

entries.title: a reassigned let no longer keeps its values in the arena
entries.body:
A `let` holding a Result that was assigned again sent every one of its
sites to the arena, and the assignment's escape flow took the function's
arena scope away with it, so a handler called from an event loop kept its
Results for the rest of the run: about 1 KB per request in a server, and
neither the retention warnings nor --deny-retention said so. Writing the
variables as `const` was the only way out.

An assignment into a local now hands the value the local's own flow
instead of an unconditional leak. A function whose reassigned `let` never
leaves the call keeps its arena scope, and each Ok/Err or by-value Result
site outside a loop gets its own stack slot, so a reassignment never
overwrites a slot an older reader still holds. Sites inside a loop, and
lets that are returned, captured, stored or self-assigned, keep their
arena placement, as before.

Tests: tests/cases/res_let_reassign
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#memory-model
Part of #1544

entries.title: keep root storage's object graph alive between wasm export calls
entries.body:
A wasm-host module can now hold an object graph across export calls.
Module-level storage declared as `const x = new Array<C | null>(n)` is a
root: after each export call the runtime traces what the roots reach, keeps
it, and releases the rest of the call's arena. When the kept region grows
past twice the live bytes plus a page, it is compacted.

Root storage is refused under threads and regions, by the native shims and
outside wasm-host. A module without root storage links exactly the bytes it
did before: the keep is compiled in only for IR that defines root storage's
arena resets.

entries.title: HmacSha256.digest allocates only the tag, and digestInto allocates nothing
entries.body:
Sha256.digestInto(out, at) and HmacSha256.digestInto(out, at) write the 32-byte digest or tag into a caller's window and allocate nothing.

- digestInto panics before writing anything if the window is outside `out`. A second digest, or an update after one, also panics.
- Sha256.digest and HmacSha256.digest are now built on digestInto, so HmacSha256.digest allocates only the 32-byte tag it returns. The inner digest it used to throw away now lives in a 32-byte field the constructor allocates, and that field is wiped right after use.
- Every intermediate is still wiped, and tests/wipes/crypto.js pins HmacSha256.digestInto's wipes under -O2.
- The `Arena.used()` checks pin that digestInto allocates nothing and that digest allocates only its tag.
- Each new negative program pins its own panic message in expected.stderr.
- RFC 4231 test cases 1–7 are checked through digestInto against the published tags.

docs/security/crypto-k1.md (K1-7), std/README.md and the guide describe the new calls. tests/nish-cmp.js declares, program by program, the IR moved by HmacSha256's wider layout.

entries.title: let the docs hero terminal take a command

The docs site's hero terminal now takes typed commands. `nish`, `--help`
and `--version` print the compiler's real output, captured at build time and

Nothing loads before it is asked for. site.js only makes the terminal take
input, and imports the shell on the first key; the shell imports the game
when the command is entered. site.js grows by under 400 B gzipped and
theme.css by under 250 B, both pinned by tests. On touch devices the terminal
takes input through a hidden field, and the line is submitted through a form
so that a soft keyboard's Go key runs it.

stale, hand-edited or extra output, and on any machine path in what is served.

entries.title: install.sh puts nish on PATH in the shell's startup file
entries.body:
The one-liner used to end by printing an `export PATH=` line to paste, and
the next thing nearly every user typed was `nish`, into `command not found`.
It now adds the install's bin/ to PATH in the startup file of the shell
$SHELL names: ~/.zshrc for zsh (under $ZDOTDIR when set), ~/.bashrc for bash
on Linux and, on macOS, whichever of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and
~/.profile a login bash already reads, conf.d/nish.fish for fish, and
~/.profile for any other shell. It says which file it changed and the
`source` line that brings it into the terminal the install ran from.

The line sits between `# >>> nish >>>` markers and is written once: a
reinstall, `nish upgrade`, or a directory already on PATH writes nothing,
and --uninstall takes the block for that install out of every file it may
have gone into, leaving other lines and other installs' blocks alone.
Startup files that are symlinks stay symlinks. --no-modify-path or
NISH_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 leaves every file untouched; scripts/fetch-seed.sh
sets it, so fetching a seed never puts build/seed/bin on a developer's PATH.

entries.title: plan WP56, generators whose memory stays flat
entries.body:
A program that reads a large spec and writes thousands of files keeps
every string it built until main returns: s = s + t keeps each
intermediate, and appending to any builder older than a loop pass
refuses that pass its arena scope. The design note plans to measure
that first, document the shapes that already stay flat (a function per
file, an arena block, a region per target), then add builder() from
nish:string, whose bytes live on a stack outside the arena that the
compiler releases at every exit of a scope that makes a builder, a write
handle to flush it, and diagnostics that point at it. Design only; the
owner's decisions are recorded in its section 10.

entries.title: warn when an unbounded loop keeps what each pass allocates (NL9018)
entries.body:
A new performance warning, NL9018, names a loop whose passes keep what they allocate when nothing bounds how many passes run: a request loop on Http1Server whose handler builds a temporary per request, a `while (running)` poll loop, an accept loop. Before this, only `--explain-memory` and `--emit-arena` showed that memory piling up, and nothing warned.

The warning reads the same `accumulates` fact `--emit-arena` writes, and keeps only the temporaries that really pile up:
- the loop has no bound it can see;
- the site's pass can continue;
- its value is not kept on purpose.

One warning per loop names the first such allocation, why the pass has no scope, and the rewrite: move the per-pass work into a `using a = arena()` block, which the compiler checks.

A loop counts as bounded when its top-level `&&` chain has an order comparison and its condition calls nothing but pure numeric conversions. A `for...of` counts as bounded unless its body extends the collection it walks. A site from which every path leaves the outermost unbounded loop does not count.

NL9018 is a retention finding: `--deny-retention` makes it NL2462. `--no-warn-performance` silences it. It changes no byte of the IR.

Five loops in the compiler's own source had the shape and now release their per-pass memory: capability-lock, discover's import read, emit-ts-records, generics' chain arguments, and the package-root walk. The compiler's output is unchanged.
metrics: an Http1Server loop with a per-request string grows past 256 kB over 20,000 requests; the arena-block rewrite stays within 256 kB (tests/run.js, shard 6)

entries.title: propose WP57, module-scoped names
entries.body:
A private function's name must be unique across the whole program, because
the emitted symbol is global and the whole-program fact table is keyed by it,
even though name lookup is already per module. The design note proposes
three stages: qualify a private function's or generic template's symbol by
its module path only when it would clash, so no program that compiles today
moves its IR; the owner's options for exported names that clash inside one
package, which are the C surface; and module-scoped class and interface
names, sized across every place that reaches a struct by name. Design only;
the rule is unchanged, and the docs that state it now link the proposal.

entries.title: load YAML into a JsonDocument about a fifth faster

entries.title: let a discriminated union be a generic's type argument
entries.body:
A discriminated union can now be a type argument like any other type. `Box<Shape>`, `Stack<Shape>`,
`Result<Shape, E>`, `Result<T, Shape>`, a generic function or method whose
`T` binds to a union, and `getOrInsert` / `reserve` on a `Map<K, Shape>` all
compile and run natively. A fallible function that returns an IR node no
longer needs a hand-written wrapper class: `(): Result<Schema, ParseError>`
just works.

Generics are monomorphised and a union is one `%union.tagged*`, so
`Box<Shape>` lowers to the same IR as a hand-written `ShapeBox`. A variant
enters its union at every generic payload site, through the checker's single
existing conversion, a pointer recast. Those sites are a constructor or
method parameter of type `T`, `Ok(...)` / `Err(...)`, a `T[]`, and either arm
of a `??` or a ternary. A generic call whose `T` is already bound to an
interface now also accepts a class that implements it.

These stay refused, each with its own code:
- a union as a `Set` element or a `Map` key
- a generic class as a variant (NL2522)
- an arm narrowed through a generic field (NL2534)
- a union type argument left to inference (NL2172)
- a constraint a union cannot meet (NL2328)
- typed JSON (NL2486)
- `nish:secret` (NL2428)
- the C header and N-API boundary (NL4009)

NL2533 is retired. Every positive case is also pinned under `-O2` escape and
arena placement, `-g`, wasm32 and `--emit-dts`.

entries.title: set inline code as a lightly tinted word, not a ringed chip
entries.body:
The reference pages run a dozen inline code spans to a paragraph, and
Scalar's 1px ring around each one turned that prose into a row of pills.
Inline code is now a faint neutral tint with no ring, slightly smaller and
with less side padding, the way GitHub and MDN set it; a grey tint, unlike
a violet one, does not compete with the links. A span that wraps closes
both its ends, a long path may break rather than widen a phone-width page,
linked code keeps a link's colour, and a table head or callout gets a

entries.title: bound the root-storage trace to the arena and the static data
entries.body: Root storage's compactor traced the kept graph as linear memory said it was, and a page can write all of linear memory: a forged root slot or pointer field made the next compaction read and rewrite memory outside the arena, and a forged array length walked until a bare trap. The trace now bounds every pointer to the arena (or, for a string, the static data) and every length to its block, and refuses a forgery with a NishPanic of kind panic before it moves anything. WH-10 is fixed in docs/security/wasm-host.md.
metrics: 1.00x on the graph drive (20,000 steps, 9,999 compactions; noise band +-5%); +745 bytes of wasm for a module with root storage
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: warn when a function keeps per-call memory no scope releases
entries.body:
A new performance warning, NL9019, reports a function that answers no
memory but keeps an allocation of its own, when a loop pass that releases
nothing calls it directly. Each call keeps one more allocation, so the
memory grows with every pass, however small the function looks. The fix
belongs in the function: give each value its own `const`, wrap the work in
`using a = arena()`, or keep what must outlive the call in a region.
`--deny-retention` turns NL9019 into an error, along with NL9002, NL9003,
NL9011, NL9016 and NL9018.

NL9019 judges only the loop's direct callees, and each one only on its own
allocations. Memory kept deeper in the call chain is not NL9019's to report;
`--explain-memory` lists it. A direct callee that runs its work only once,
behind a guard, still warns. Constructors are not reported. A loop nested
inside an arena block, or inside a scoped outer pass, counts as released.

Ok(..) and Err(..) built in a loop now count as visible allocations, so
NL9003 and NL9016 report a boxed Result dropped on every pass.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: drop internal work-package references from diagnostics and generated files
entries.body:
Diagnostics NL4010 and NL4011, the comments the compiler writes into async
.ll files, C headers, N-API sidecars, wasm loaders and the --emit-ts storage
file, and the nish/vite error for a loader without loadSync no longer name
internal planning notes; they say the same thing in plain words, and the

reference and the guide pages that quote these messages move with them.

entries.title: run the hero once and leave the terminal's prompt waiting
entries.body:
The landing page's hero looped forever, and holding its terminal still
while it was used (hover, focus, a click) kept fighting the loop. Now the
sequence plays once: the source is typed, flows through the compiler to
its targets, runs, and the terminal keeps the formula with a blinking
prompt on the next line, ready for a command. Every part ends on its
finished frame; only the ambient glow and the compiler's ring keep moving.
The hover and hold logic is gone, and the size budgets the docs tests pin
for the terminal fall back to 500 B for site.js and 250 B for theme.css.

`nish break` in the terminal now grows the game out of the terminal's box
to the full screen, and closing it shrinks it back into the terminal
before it leaves the page. It does not move under reduced motion or with
no terminal to grow from.

docs/site/break is rebuilt from examples/break-web with the current
compiler; game.wasm is unchanged.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: put WP34's phase two on its roadmap page
entries.body:
The roadmap page tracked only the network stack's stages, while the note's §8 lists the compiler items the later phases owe. Every one of them is now built, most under packages of their own (WP46, WP49, WP50), and nothing on the page said so.

The page gains §8's items N7 to N14 as ticked boxes, each with the pull request or package that built it, and §8 of the note now says its items are built and that their state lives on the roadmap page.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: WP54, async on wasm with the page as the executor (design only)
entries.body:
WP49 refuses async under the wasm profiles until a host loop is designed, and WP50 keeps NL2652 and names the design it would take, WP49's state machine with the page as its executor, as "its own note". No such note existed, so both pointed at nothing.

This is that note, proposed and design only. The lowering carries over unchanged. A host import may answer a promise, which becomes a wait token; the page's event loop does the waiting; a settled promise resumes the module through one generated export that runs from the microtask queue, so WP50's re-entry rule holds; spawn and awaitAll keep their meaning; sleep becomes a loader import, and readable and writable stay refused. The one open design question is the region WP49 gives every task, which the freestanding profiles cannot make: a fixed pool for a page, so its views never go stale, or a malloc for a Worker.

It argues its own scope down. A page that drives a module does not need it, because WP50's page already awaits each promise and calls an export. The case for building it is a service that must run on Cloudflare Workers, which run JavaScript or wasm and nothing else, so the first question for the owner is whether to build it at all. JSPI is weighed and not recommended, because a function that suspends under it has a TypeScript reading that cannot wait, and the checker loses sight of every place a task may suspend. Nothing is measured yet: each cost is stated as what a stage must measure.

The note gets its roadmap page, its route under "In progress and proposed", its rows in docs/README.md, MASTER_PLAN.md and the roadmap overview, and WP49's and WP50's pointers to it.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: make the README a short tour and drop the owner wording
entries.body:
The README is now a taste of the language -- install, a first program, the
IR it compiles to -- followed by a table of contents and one short section
per area, each linking to its guide page, and a table of where to read next.

Pages, security records and bench notes no longer narrate one person's
decisions: an undecided item is an open question, and a settled one says what
was decided. The last .claude/plans files are removed. The npm package ships
only scripts/build.sh and scripts/postinstall.mjs from scripts/, rather than
every development script.

entries.title: CUBIC congestion control for QUIC (WP39 G5)
entries.body: Adds RFC 9438 CUBIC to std/net/quic-recovery.ts and makes it the default controller (QUIC_RECOVERY_DEFAULT). NewReno stays available as QUIC_RECOVERY_NEWRENO; QuicServerConfig.congestion picks one. Tests that pin exact NewReno window traces name the pin with a reason. The HTTP/3 server slot budget moves +72 bytes for the controller choice and CUBIC state.

entries.title: one handler for HTTP/1.1, 2 and 3 with Alt-Svc (WP39 G7)
entries.body:
Adds nish/net/http-server: one HttpServer with one request pool, one poll loop and one Router serves HTTP/1.1, cleartext HTTP/2, HTTP/2 over TLS and HTTP/3. Every request comes out of the same take and is answered through the same send, sendFields, start, write and end, whichever version carried it. Once an HTTP/3 listener is configured, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2-over-TLS responses carry Alt-Svc.

Every carrier screens out a plain CONNECT (501), OPTIONS * (204), a head past maxFields (431) and a body past maxBody (413) before take. bodyTimeout applies on every version and idleTimeout on HTTP/2. Bodies grow in tiers, so a held body costs at most maxBody + 3T, where T = min(65536, maxBody).
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: add object graphs in an arena block to WP56 as S5
entries.body:
Inside `using a = arena()`, a call to any function that stores an
allocation is refused (NL2424), so a class whose constructor does
`this.parts = []` cannot be made inside the block, and generators keep
one graph outside it, cleared between files by hand-written `reset`
methods. WP56 gains a sixth stage, S5, and decision D7: an object graph
made inside the block belongs to the block, so stores into memory the
block allocated are admitted while every outward route stays refused.
Applying the same analysis to parallel bodies and `scope()` tasks is
deferred to its own design note. Design only: nothing is built.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: propose WP59, the wasm arena in a second, unexported memory
entries.body:
WH-10's fix bounds every pointer and length the root-storage trace reads,
but a page that owns the exported memory can still forge a pointer that
lands inside the arena and scramble its own kept graph. The design note
proposes the structural fix: the arena, the kept graph and root storage
move to a second wasm memory the module never exports, while exported
storage, views(), the rings and the exchange area for crossings stay in
the exported one. It corrects WH-10's claim that views() and the rings
need nothing from the arena, citing the loader paths that do. It records
the LLVM 18 experiment: clang and wasm-ld emit one memory, so the second
is added by a post-link rewrite before wasm-opt. It prices each copy at a
crossing, tabulates engine support with a single-memory fallback, and
stages the work in four steps: the rewrite, the crossings behind a flag,
the forge test and a size and speed budget measured like #1571, and the
security record. Design only; no code changes. WH-10 stays Fixed and now
points at WP59.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: cheaper string runs past non-ASCII bytes
entries.body:
A JSON string's text run used to leave the vector loop at every byte of 128 or more and walk one UTF-8 sequence at a time. On twitter.json that walk was about 70% of the text kernel's cost. The SSE2 path now checks a whole 16-byte block of multi-byte text at once, using compares and shifts only. The check flags a continuation that disagrees with the leads before it, a lead no RFC 3629 form starts with, and the second byte of an overlong, surrogate or above-U+10FFFF form. A flagged block goes to the existing scalar step, so invalid UTF-8 still stops at the same byte and the tokenizer reports the same error offset.

The AVX2 path hands a run to the SSE2 block check at its first high byte. Once a block is ASCII again it takes the run back into its own 32-byte loop. The hand-offs are tail calls both ways, so the stack stays flat. NEON and wasm are unchanged.

runtime-bytes.c grows from 1,525 to 1,891 bytes, so RUNTIME_BYTES_TEXT_BUDGET moves from 1,536 to 2,048, a raise recorded with its gain in docs/wp7-runtime.md. tests/simd/byte-runs.c now puts every valid and invalid UTF-8 form at every offset of a block, with the limit on every byte, and holds the scalar, SSE2 and AVX2 paths to one reference.
metrics: callgrind Ir per document, (N=10 - N=1)/9, same checksums: tokenize twitter.json 12,332,881 -> -8.13%, citm_catalog -1.09%, canada 0.00%; held-out api payload (4.3% non-ASCII) -1.87%; a long ASCII string after one early non-ASCII byte +1.93%, a long ASCII string -4.03%. Wall clock, 15 interleaved rounds: every change inside the byte-identical-copy noise band (twitter band 8.44%).

entries.title: fit the docs site's break game to a phone and give it one menu
entries.body:
On a phone the docs site's hidden breakout game ran edge to edge, so the
side the frame is open on, under the paddle, looked cut off by the

corner. The canvas is now sized to the frame's own shape inside the

only a finger steers the paddle. Keyboard play is unchanged.

The landing page's "NISH" no longer unfolds into "Native Instruction
Static Host" on every load: it opens only while hovered or focused (a
tap focuses it), so the hero has less moving at once.

entries.title: parse a JSON number in one pass
entries.body:
The tokenizer's number scan now folds the digits into the mantissa as it passes them. It takes eight at a time where eight bytes remain, with a SWAR check that rejects any byte that is not an ASCII digit. It keeps the mantissa, scale and digit count on the tokenizer, so `numberF64` and `numberI64` read those instead of walking the text a second time. Only a number of more than 19 digits, or one whose exponent passes the cap, is walked again or handed to `parseFloat`. The doubles are bit for bit those `parseFloat` gives. A short run ends before its eighth byte, so that byte is read first, and only a run that reaches it pays for the eight-byte read.

`JsonTokenizer` gains four number fields, which widens the C header of every program that reads it. The nish-cmp corpus declares each moved program and file.

Wall clock (median, 21 interleaved rounds, band from byte-identical binaries): canada -31.9% (band 1.5%), citm -12.6% (band 1.0%), typed citm -13.0% (band 2.6%); twitter, api and the 242-byte body within their bands (31 rounds).

entries.title: document package.json and the capability lockfile from JSON Schemas
entries.body:
Every field Nish reads in a package.json is now described once, in schemas/package.schema.json. That covers the nish field's capabilities, noPanic and host, and Node's exports, engines and version as Nish reads them. The capability lockfile is described in schemas/capabilities-lock.schema.json.

The reference renders a page from each schema under Reference -> Configuration files, through @amritk/generate-markdown (the renderer behind `mjst markdown`), so the page and an editor's hover text say the same thing. Each field names the error a mistake in it gets.

The sandbox guide gains a section on granting a dependency its capabilities, the basic case its narrowing section assumed. The modules and interop guides link to the new reference page.
tests: every package.json and lockfile under tests/ validates against its schema
except the fixtures the compiler refuses for a shape reason.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: write a typed object's keys as one pre-escaped copy
entries.body:
jsonEncode of a class now quotes and escapes each field's key once, at
compile time, into a string constant ("name":), and calls the new
@internal JsonWriter.keyQuoted, which copies it after the comma in one
step when the writer is minified and has room. Any other way (an
indenting writer, a full buffer, a failed or misused writer) it runs
key(name), so the bytes written and the failed code are always key's.
Before, every key went through the same byte-at-a-time escape scan as a
runtime string. JsonWriter.i32 and i64 also count their digits by
compares rather than divides. The output is byte-identical.

The profile came first: on main, key escaping and the per-key state
checks were the largest per-field cost in typed serialize. After the
change keyQuoted is about a quarter of either profile, JsonWriter.i64
30% of citm's, and jsonWriterPutString (escaping string values) a third
of the API page's. bench/json-api is a new non-bench-shaped program, a
page of twenty user records, so the gain is shown outside citm.
metrics: citm serialize 1.38x to 1.40x at the minimum (bands 0.2-8.8% on minimums); json-api page 1.29x at the minimum (band 2.3%), 1.22x at the median (band 1.6%); callgrind -24.0% (citm, 14.13M to 10.74M) and -13.9% (json-api, 188,879 to 162,647) Ir per document
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: forEach on arrays, Map and Set
entries.body:
`xs.forEach(f)` on `T[]` and `readonly T[]`, `m.forEach((v, k) => …)` on
`Map<K, V>` and `s.forEach((v) => …)` on `Set<T>` now compile. Until now
there was no way to visit a Map's key and value together.

They use the same statically-known-callee templates as `map` and `filter`
(std/array.ts, std/collections.ts). Each callback is its own instance, called
directly and inlined after -O2, with no closure and no allocation. An array
forEach visits indices below the length the array had when the call began,
as `Array.prototype.forEach` does. A Map or Set forEach runs the table walk
`for...of` uses, in insertion order, and reads each value from the walk's
slot, with no `get` and no second probe per entry. A callback that pushes,
pops, stores, sets, deletes or clears on the receiver prints what Node
prints.

The answer is void, and using it is an error. An array callback takes at
most `(x, i)`, a Map callback `(v, k)` (NL2771) and a Set callback `(v)`
(NL2772). A callback that assigns a local of the enclosing function is still
NL2586, and the message now points to a `for...of` loop for accumulating.

At -O2, with receivers whose length is only known at run time: an array
forEach is 18 instructions, the same count as its `for...of` loop. Map
forEach is 92 against 112 for `for...of` with `m.get(k)`, and Set forEach is
78 against 89.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: less fixed work per JSON token
entries.body:
The tokenizer's `next()` now switches on the byte first. A quote, colon, comma or closer, which make up most of a document's tokens, costs one switch and one test of what the grammar wants; anything else goes on to the old switch on `want`. The innermost open container is kept in a field, so a comma or closer reads no depth stack. A sticky error is answered from a `want` state that `fail` sets, so the hot path no longer tests `failed`. The blank skip and the byte read share one bound. A string finds its byte limit with one comparison against a precomputed `stringFrom`. `stringInto` copies a string with no escapes in one `copyBytes`, and copies the plain runs between escapes whole. Every error code and offset is unchanged, and trailing commas, a surrogate pair between plain runs and a run ending at the window's end are pinned.

`JsonTokenizer` gains two i32 fields, widening it from 112 to 120 bytes; the nish-cmp corpus entries that declare its layout already cover the programs this moves. The same change corrects #1589's nish-cmp declaration to "ForEach on arrays, Map and Set", the capitalized spelling its changelog entry renders. nish-cmp matches that text case-sensitively, so the lowercase spelling had turned main's nish-cmp red.
metrics: callgrind Ir per document, base -> branch, same checksums: twitter -11.2%, citm -5.6%, canada -7.6%, typed citm -5.1%, typed-reuse citm -5.1%, held-out metrics -9.3%, held-out api -33.0%, 242-byte body -5.5%. Wall clock (median, 21 interleaved rounds pinned to one core, band from byte-identical binaries): twitter -13.1% (band 1.4%), api -21.1% (band 2.0%), typed-reuse citm -10.8% (band 4.6%), canada -4.6% (band 3.3%), metrics -4.0% (band 0.8%); citm, typed citm and the 242-byte body within their bands.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: AtomicI32Array and AtomicI64Array, n atomics in one buffer
entries.body:
`nish/threads` gains two classes that hold n atomic counters in one buffer:
`AtomicI32Array` and `AtomicI64Array`. They are for per-route request counts,
histogram bins and per-shard metrics. Each has the methods of `AtomicI32` and
`AtomicI64` with the element index first: `load`, `store`, `add`, `sub`,
`min`, `max`, `exchange` and `compareExchange`. Each compiles to one inline
sequentially consistent `atomicrmw`, `cmpxchg` or atomic load or store on an
element of the buffer. The index is range-checked like an array index, so an
out-of-range or negative index, or a negative length, stops the program. The
arrays reach a scope's tasks and a parallel body by the routes an `AtomicI32`
does, and are refused where it is refused. The buffer starts on a 64-byte
boundary with slack before and after it, so the lines its elements sit on are
shared with no other allocation.

An array of `AtomicI32` objects puts each counter in its own small allocation,
interleaved with the array's own blocks. par-histogram-atomic's sixteen bins
landed on four cache lines, and the array header could share a line with bin
0. Rust's `[AtomicI32; 16]` and Go's `[16]atomic.Int32` keep all sixteen on
one line. That layout was the whole gap: the add itself was already inlined,
and removing the bounds check changed nothing. The kernel now keeps its bins
in one `AtomicI32Array`, the layout its twins use, with the same work and
checksum.

The threads guide, LANGUAGE.md, the IR cookbook and the reference document the
new classes. Every program that imports nish/threads gets a new `threads.ll`
and a `struct AtomicI32Array;` declaration in its header; its own module is
unchanged. NL2515's message now lists the new constructors.
metrics: par-histogram-atomic par 114/120 -> 65.5/73.8 ms (min/median); Nish / fastest Rust twin 1.586x-1.950x -> 0.932x-1.059x by min over 3 runs of `node bench/run.mjs --only par`, bands 4.5%-8.5%

entries.title: cut Router.match's instructions per request for every route kind
entries.body:
One pass hashes and splits a path for the static table, so a miss goes to
the tree without reading the path again; a method of up to seven bytes is
matched as one packed word; and the byte compare checks its two ranges once
and then reads unchecked. Answers, parameters and limits are unchanged.
metrics: Ir per match -8.0% to -22.0% by route kind (callgrind, deterministic, band 0); TFB async plaintext 6502 -> 6470 Ir/req, json 8223 -> 8203 (explicit entry band +-4)

entries.title: record the JSON tokenizer result
entries.body:
docs/BENCHMARKS.md carries a fresh "JSON against other languages" record, taken with `bench/json-compare/run.mjs --rounds 9 --mb 128 --record` on the source of fb4b625e. That source includes the UTF-8 block check (#1588), the one-pass number parse (#1590) and the per-token cuts (#1600). simdjson, yyjson, RapidJSON, serde_json and Go all ran.

Below the record, a held-out table gives the tokenize workload's callgrind instructions per document, base f8e21091 against fb4b625e, with checksums equal. It covers payloads the tuning never saw: a float-heavy metrics document, a string-heavy API response with non-ASCII text and escapes, and the 242-byte `bench/json-tokenizer` body. `bench/json-compare/heldout.mjs` generates the first two from fixed seeds, pins all three by SHA-256 (checked before every measurement and by `--check`), and prints Ir per document for one compiler or for two with `--base`. docs/wp38-simd.md records which of S6d's per-value cuts were built and by which pull requests.

entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: emit self-recursive checked sums as a loop
entries.body:
A function whose every recursive return is `X + self(args)` over the checked i32 `+` (fib, a tree sum, a count of nodes) now compiles to one loop instead of a tree of calls. LLVM folds such a return into a loop only when the `+` is a plain add. Since signed overflow became a checked panic, the overflow check defeated it, and fib made twice the calls C and Rust make. Its code per call was already identical to C with the same check.

The loop keeps every check. The header adds the running sum unchecked, and while every step is non-negative a sign test proves that nothing wrapped. A step that fails the test makes one ordinary call and returns the checked adds the recursion would have made. So a program panics on exactly the input, and with exactly the output, it did before. The only difference is that a recursion deep enough to exhaust the stack now completes. The proof sits beside the emitter in src/emit-accumulate.ts.

Eligible functions are plain i32 functions of the module with no captures, loops, switch, arena scope or stack-allocated locals. In `self(args) + Y`, Y must be a number literal or a parameter. Everything else, and every function under --no-elision or a debug build, compiles as before.
metrics: fib(40) 1.68x -> 0.99x / 1.06x of Rust -O3 on two interleaved runs (Nish 329 / 348 ms min, noise band ~6%); a class-node tree sum, median 318 -> 191 ms over 15 interleaved runs (band ~6%)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: serve drives the HTTP/1 server directly instead of through HttpHandler (WP49 stage 6)
entries.body:
nish/net/serve now runs Http1Server from its own readiness loop instead of
going through HttpHandler. Each connection slot keeps one request whose head
and spans are the parser's own, read in place until the answer is sent; the
request's task still copies it before its first await, so every handler
keeps its own copy. The per-request head copy into a pool and the handler's
general-purpose response paths are gone from the serve path.

Answered bytes, pipelining order, timeouts, the per-request deadline,
hang-up cancellation, 500 for a wrong Response, 503 past the in-flight cap,
the maxRequests drain and the ServeStats meanings are unchanged, and the API
stays source-compatible. HttpHandler is unchanged for its other users. Each
open connection now holds its own request record (about 400 B), so peak
memory grows with connections, not with load.
metrics: Ir/request -2.2% plaintext async (6520 -> 6374), -1.3% json async (8229 -> 8122), plain serve app -3.5% /health (6740 -> 6504) and -3.2% /notes/17 (7305 -> 7070) (callgrind, deterministic); req/s within the 3-round band; peak RSS at plaintext c=16384 26.2 -> 32.5 MiB (+24%, bounded by connections)

entries.title: design and measure dynamic dispatch over interfaces (WP60)
entries.body:
Adds the WP60 design note, which designs and measures `Dyn<I>`: a value that holds any class implementing an interface, whose method calls lower to a per-place `switch` of direct calls (WP51's machinery, with classes as the members). It never uses a vtable or an object header. The note also adds the roadmap page and points the WP25, FAQ and validator notes at it. WP54 and WP59 were taken, so this is WP60.

The recommendation is to ship stage 1 now, gate stage 2 and gate stage 3:
- Stage 1: interface method signatures, used statically through `<T extends I>`. No IR moves for any program that compiles today.
- Stage 2: `Dyn<I>` in locals, parameters and returns. It lands only when its own build passes its gate. On the modelled surface it is 0.72x the hand `kind`/`switch` in geomean, but one case (a set of two chosen at random per call) runs at 2.21x.
- Stage 3: stored `Dyn<I>`, as one tagged word. It meets the size invariant on x86_64, aarch64 and wasm32, but measured 1.18x on arrays. It is gated after stage 2.
- The vtable is rejected: 1.88x in geomean.

Every figure was measured on one 4-core machine (best of 7, interleaved and rotated), with checksums checked across variants. The programs and the runner are in the note's appendix.
metrics: 0.72x geomean over 15 register-form cases (worst 2.21x), band ±3.3%; stored tagged word 1.18x on array rows, band ±2.6%

entries.title: destructuring declarations over objects and arrays
entries.body:
`const` and `let` declarations, and a `for...of` head, now accept destructuring patterns.

- An object pattern works over a class or interface value: `const { x, y: py } = p`. Each name is exactly one field load, and the struct is never copied.
- An array pattern works over `T[]`, holes included: `const [a, , c] = xs`. Each element is read with the same bounds check and panic as `xs[i]`. TypeScript would give `undefined` for an element past the end; Nish panics, because it has no `undefined`.

A plain name, `this`, or a field path such as `o.items` is read directly, so the pattern compiles to the same IR as its hand-written reads. Any other receiver (a call, an index, a `?.` chain or a `for...of` element) is evaluated once into a hidden local. After `opt -O2` its IR is identical too.

Every other form is still refused, each with its own diagnostic (NL2773-NL2785):
- assignment patterns;
- defaults, rest elements and nested patterns;
- a key that is not a field, or that names a method;
- a pattern over `T | null`, `T | undefined`, a Map, a Set or a string.

Parameter patterns, `var` patterns and top-level `const` patterns stay refused. A module constant is a compile-time value folded into each use, so at run time there is nothing for a pattern to read.

`--emit-ts` passes the pattern through, and the differential run agrees with Node. An object that is only destructured is still stack-allocated.
metrics: compiling src/compile.ts, 10 interleaved runs against main: wall time 2.139 s vs 2.177 s (base copy 2.175 s, inside noise); peak RSS +38 KiB (0.002%, noise band ~250 KiB); IR for src/compile.ts byte-identical (137/137 .ll); nish-cmp corpus 0 undeclared differences

entries.title: pin every panicking acc_* case against --no-elision byte for byte
entries.body: Each tests/cases/acc_*.panics lists the runs of its program that must panic, one argv per line. The acc section builds every such program twice, as is and with --no-elision, runs each listed argv under both, and compares stdout, stderr and the exit status byte for byte, so the loop's overflow is pinned against the recursion it replaces rather than against a hand-copied message. Guards keep the comparison meaningful: the default build must contain the loop and the reference must not, every listed run must panic, and a sidecar must name at least one run; negatives show each guard and a mismatch fail.

entries.title: commit the tree-sum benchmark with a free-function and a method kernel
entries.body: bench/treesum.{ts,c,go,rs} walks one complete depth-20 tree of heap nodes 60 times, in two kernels timed as their own rows: `treesum/fn`, the free function `t.value + sum(t.left) + sum(t.right)` that docs/wp9-optimisation.md measured, and `treesum/method`, the same walk as a `TreeNode.sum()` method. The tree-sum figure in the wp9 note can now be reproduced, and the method kernel is the target for emitting self-recursive checked-sum methods as a loop. Node values are masked to 10 bits, so no sum leaves i32; the root takes the pass number, so no compiler can hoist the walk out of the pass loop. Every language prints the same checksum per kernel. treesum is timed but not instruction-counted.

entries.title: cut serve's answer path and hold a request record only from parse to copy
entries.body:
serve's answer path keeps each slot's connection in its exchange, runs a send on without looking the connection up again, masks its queue ring, and reads the clock once per answer pass instead of once per answer. A connection no longer keeps a request record for its whole life: a record is taken from a pool when a head is parsed and given back once the request's task has copied it, once it answered 503, or once the connection closed first, so idle keep-alive connections hold none. This undoes most of the peak RSS that reading in place added (SERVE-13), at no cost in instructions per request. Every answered byte is unchanged.

net_serve_raw pins whole answers byte for byte (200 text and JSON, 404, a wrong Response as 500 and the request after it, HEAD, a 503 past the in-flight cap, a pipelined batch), and net_serve_idle_record fails when a slot keeps its record. docs/security/serve.md gives SERVE-13's bound with pooled records and each slot's pending array.

entries.title: say that a record type is always a declared name
entries.body: An inline object type, `(p: { x: i32 }) => p.x`, and a `type` alias of one, `type Point = { x: i32; y: i32 }`, are refused by the parser with "expected a type name, found `{`" (NL0001), but nothing said so: a reader coming from TypeScript met the syntax error with no rule behind it. The reference now states the rule under "Interfaces and object literals", "Type aliases" and "Coming from TypeScript": a record type is identified by its declaration, so two interfaces with the same fields are two types, and the only widening is a class to an interface it `implements`. The classes-and-interfaces guide page shows the refusal and the fix, an `interface`.

entries.title: propose WP61, typed JSON constraints and coercion in one pass
entries.body:
WP61 proposes two additions to nish/json-typed, both checked inside
jsonDecode's single walk over the bytes.

Constraints (minLength, pattern, minimum, enum, format and the rest) are
declared on the class and checked as each value is read, with a new
decode code and the offset of the offending value. A class that declares
none generates byte-identical IR to today.

An opt-in coercion mode never fails: a value with a defined conversion is
converted, anything else takes the field's default, unknown keys are
ignored, and malformed JSON or a limit stops reading (the limits still
bound the work) with the unread fields defaulted. What went wrong stays
readable in reason, errorAt and stopped. Whether the repair log is always
on is decided by a benchmark gate. The design borrows from mjst's
coercing parsers. The JSON Schema generator is WP62.

entries.title: emit self-recursive checked-sum methods as a loop
entries.body:
A method of a non-generic, non-atomic class of its module now qualifies for the checked-sum loop when its steps call that same method on a receiver of its own class, as a tree walk's `this.value + l + right.sum()` does. Nish binds every method call statically, so such a call reaches this very body, and the loop treats the receiver as one more parameter: a header phi rebound on each step, evaluated after the step's X and before its arguments, as the call evaluates it. The cold path calls the method on the receiver the loop has reached. A field is never Y in `self(args) + Y`, so nothing is read after a call the loop skips. The proof beside the emitter now points its Y sentence at the recorder's argument in src/accumulate.ts.

Calls through a function-valued field, a same-named method of another class, a generic class's method and a field Y all stay recursion. tests/cases/acc_method_overflow.panics runs every overflow case, one of them on a rebound receiver, against --no-elision byte for byte. acc_ineligible's method case moved into acc_method, now that it loops. mem_callee_scope's `Element.length`, the cookbook entry and AWFY's list now loop; nish-cmp declares each.
metrics: no gain outside the noise. treesum/method median 269.6 / 223.4 ms → 263.3 / 208.3 ms over two interleaved rounds. Same-code rows drifted 6–17 % between rounds, so the 2 % and 7 % deltas are inside the band. fib held at 0.92x of Rust (0.92x / 0.89x before).

entries.title: propose WP62, Nish classes from a JSON Schema
entries.body:
WP62 proposes a generator that turns a JSON Schema (2020-12, with draft-07
and OpenAPI 3.x normalised first) into Nish classes, keeping as much of the
schema as the target can hold. A keyword-by-keyword table says where each
keyword lands: description, title, examples, deprecated, $comment and
externalDocs become JSDoc; default becomes the field's initializer, or a
derived default that satisfies the field's constraints, with the schema's
own value kept as @default; validation keywords become WP61's constraints;
$ref becomes one shared class and a tagged oneOf a union. A keyword the
classes cannot enforce is refused with a diagnostic naming its schema
path, never silently weakened.

Its first stage is two typed JSON prerequisites: an optional field whose
default the constructor assigns ([], new Map(), new C(), new JsonNumber()),
and per-class unknown-key handling. The design borrows from mjst's
validation generators.
